description: A reading comprehension pack for KS3 Earth and atmosphere. Passages use source-based science explanations and questions that test retrieval, inference, explanation, data interpretation and evaluation.

data.sourceTitle: Earth Layers and the Air Around Us
data.targetTitle: Earth Layers and the Air Around Us
data.sourcePassage: Earth is approximately spherical, although it is slightly wider at the equator than from pole to pole. It is made from layers: the thin solid crust, the very thick mantle, the outer core and the inner core. The crust is the layer people live on, and surface rocks are part of it. Around Earth is the atmosphere, a mixture of gases held close by gravity. Most air is near the surface because gravity keeps gas particles more crowded together. Dry air is mostly nitrogen, with oxygen making up about one fifth. Carbon dioxide is only a very small percentage of dry air, but it matters because it is involved in photosynthesis and the greenhouse effect.

questions.question: Which Earth layer is the thin solid outer layer?
questions.modelAnswer: The crust is the thin solid outer layer.

questions.question: Which gas is most common in dry air?
questions.modelAnswer: Nitrogen is the most common gas in dry air.

questions.question: Why is most air found close to Earth's surface?
questions.modelAnswer: Most air is close to the surface because gravity pulls gas particles towards Earth, keeping them more crowded together.

questions.question: Why can carbon dioxide matter even though there is little of it in dry air?
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide matters because it is a greenhouse gas and is also used by plants and algae in photosynthesis.

questions.question: Why are classroom diagrams of Earth's layers often not to scale?
questions.modelAnswer: They often exaggerate thin layers such as the crust so important features are visible and easier to understand.

data.sourcePassage: The natural greenhouse effect is a process that keeps Earth warmer than it would otherwise be. Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms Earth's surface. The warm surface emits infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases such as water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide absorb some of this radiation and re-emit it in different directions. The natural greenhouse effect is useful because it keeps Earth warm enough for life. The problem is the enhanced greenhouse effect. Human activities such as burning fossil fuels, deforestation, cement production and intensive farming increase greenhouse gas concentrations. This means more infrared radiation is absorbed and re-emitted, so more energy remains in the Earth system and average global temperature rises.

questions.question: What type of radiation is emitted by Earth's warm surface?
questions.modelAnswer: Earth's warm surface emits infrared radiation.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the natural greenhouse effect?
options: It keeps Earth warm enough for life.
questions.modelAnswer: It keeps Earth warm enough for life.

questions.question: Name two human activities that can increase greenhouse gas concentrations.
questions.modelAnswer: Burning fossil fuels and deforestation can increase greenhouse gas concentrations. Cement production and intensive farming are also valid examples.

questions.question: Explain how extra greenhouse gases can raise average global temperature.
questions.modelAnswer: Extra greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit more infrared radiation, so more energy remains in the Earth system and average global temperature rises.

questions.question: Why is it misleading to say that the greenhouse effect is always bad?
questions.modelAnswer: The natural greenhouse effect is useful because it supports life; the problem is the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by extra greenhouse gases.

data.sourcePassage: Carbon is found in many parts of the Earth system. A carbon store is a place where carbon is kept, such as the atmosphere, plants, animals, soils, oceans, fossil fuels and carbonate rocks. A carbon transfer is a process that moves carbon from one store to another. Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere because plants and algae use it to make glucose. Feeding transfers carbon from one organism to another. Respiration adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere because cells release energy from food. Combustion adds carbon dioxide when fuels are burned. Burning fossil fuels is important because it moves carbon from long-term stores into the atmosphere much faster than most natural processes would.

questions.question: What is a carbon store?
questions.modelAnswer: A carbon store is a place where carbon is kept for a period of time.

questions.question: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
questions.modelAnswer: Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

questions.question: How does feeding transfer carbon?
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon in food moves from one organism to another when an organism eats.

questions.question: Why does combustion add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere?
questions.modelAnswer: Combustion burns fuel in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Why is burning fossil fuels especially important in the carbon cycle?
questions.modelAnswer: It rapidly transfers carbon from long-term stores such as coal, oil and gas into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.

data.sourceTitle: Rocks, Weathering and the Rock Cycle
data.targetTitle: Rocks, Weathering and the Rock Cycle
data.sourcePassage: Rocks are naturally occurring materials made of minerals. At KS3, the three main rock groups are igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic. Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools and solidifies. Slow cooling underground can make large crystals, while fast cooling at the surface can make smaller crystals. Sedimentary rocks form when weathered fragments are transported, deposited in layers, compacted and cemented. They may contain layers, grains or fossils. Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are changed by heat and pressure without fully melting. Weathering breaks rock down in place. Erosion moves rock or sediment away. Transportation carries sediment, and deposition drops sediment when water, wind or ice loses energy.

questions.question: Which rock type forms when molten rock cools and solidifies?
questions.modelAnswer: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and solidifies.

questions.question: Which feature is common in sedimentary rocks?
questions.modelAnswer: Visible layers or fossils are common in sedimentary rocks.

questions.question: Explain the difference between magma and lava.
questions.modelAnswer: Magma is molten rock below Earth's surface, while lava is molten rock at the surface.

questions.question: How are weathering and erosion different?
questions.modelAnswer: Weathering breaks rock down in place, while erosion moves rock or sediment away.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to say that metamorphic rocks form by melting?
questions.modelAnswer: Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are changed by heat and pressure without fully melting; melting would produce molten rock.

data.sourcePassage: Scientists use data to study climate and environmental change, but conclusions should be cautious and evidence-based. A simplified table in the source shows carbon dioxide concentration rising from 317 ppm in 1960 to 423 ppm in 2025. Over the same period, the temperature anomaly generally increases from -0.02 degrees C to 0.95 degrees C, although one year may not fit the pattern perfectly. Correlation alone does not prove cause, so scientists also use the known mechanism: carbon dioxide absorbs and re-emits some infrared radiation. Towns can use evidence to choose climate actions. Home insulation can reduce heating emissions, public transport can reduce car journeys, tree planting can store carbon over decades, and improved drainage can reduce flood risk. Each option has benefits, limitations, costs and questions of fairness.

questions.question: What was the carbon dioxide concentration in 1960 in the simplified source data?
questions.modelAnswer: It was 317 ppm in 1960.

questions.question: Why does correlation alone not prove cause?
options: It is the same as a fair test.
Scientists also need a mechanism and other evidence.
It means data should be ignored.
questions.modelAnswer: A correlation shows two things change together, but scientists also need a mechanism and other evidence.

questions.question: Give one benefit and one limitation of home insulation.
questions.modelAnswer: Home insulation can reduce energy use and heating emissions, but it has upfront cost and may cause disruption.

questions.question: Why might improved drainage be adaptation rather than mitigation?
questions.modelAnswer: Improved drainage prepares for heavier rainfall and flood risk but does not directly reduce greenhouse gas emissions much.

questions.question: Write a cautious conclusion linking carbon dioxide and temperature from the simplified data.
questions.modelAnswer: As carbon dioxide concentration increased, temperature anomaly generally increased too. This supports a link, but scientists need long-term evidence and the greenhouse mechanism to explain cause.
